title: "äpple" sorts after "zebra" with a default sort
assumption: An accented letter sorts next to its unaccented counterpart — "äpple" belongs near "apple", not off at the end of the alphabet.

input.description: A product or name list containing a word with a diacritic, sorted with the default (non-locale-aware) string comparison.

what_goes_wrong: The default sort returns ["apple", "zebra", "äpple"] — "äpple" lands after "zebra", not next to "apple" where a human alphabetizing by the base letter would put it.
why: "ä" is U+00E4, a higher value than "z" (U+007A): the Latin-1 Supplement block, where most Western European accented letters live, comes entirely after the ASCII lowercase letters. Python's default string comparison orders by code point and JavaScript's by UTF-16 code unit (the same thing for these characters), so neither knows that "ä" is a variant of "a" in most European alphabets. Only a locale-aware collator knows that relationship.
fix: Use a locale-aware comparator for any text a human will read: Intl.Collator or String.prototype.localeCompare() in JavaScript. Python's standard library has no built-in Unicode collation; it requires either the system locale module (environment-dependent) or a third-party ICU binding.

sources.title: Unicode Standard Annex #10: Unicode Collation Algorithm

test_cases.note: their_function(a, b) as a human-order "a sorts before b" test should return false: äpple belongs before zebra. Raw `a < b` returns true here, which is the trap.
